item.title: Police come under attack during AL procession in Chittagong
item.description:
Police came under attack during a procession by the activities-banned Awami League in the Bandar area of Chittagong city on Friday, with 20 people arrested in connection with the incident.
Six police personnel, including Bandar police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Abdur Rahim, were injured in the incident, which took place around 3pm in the Taltala area of Port Connecting Road under Bandar police station.
According to police and local sources, leaders and activists of the activities-banned Awami League brought out a procession in the area on Friday afternoon. After receiving information about the procession, a police team went to the scene and attempted to stop it.
At that point, participants allegedly threw brickbats at police and smashed the glass of a police vehicle, injuring 6 police personnel, including the OC.
Police later chased the procession participants and arrested 20 people from the scene.
A case has been filed with Bandar police station over the attack on police under the Anti-Terrorism Act.
OC Abdur Rahim said brickbats were thrown at police during the procession and the glass of a police vehicle was smashed. He added that police operations to arrest the other participants were continuing.

item.title: The pink bus experience: A smoother ride, if you can catch it
Five priorities for Bangladesh ahead of COP31
item.description:
For decades, Bangladesh has stood at the frontline of climate change. Rising sea levels, cyclones, floods, salinity intrusion, and heat stress have made the country one of the most climate-vulnerable nations in the world.
Yet Bangladesh has also become one of the world's most remarkable examples of climate adaptation and resilience-building.
Discussions on Bangladesh’s climate priorities ahead of COP31 took place during the 64th meeting of the Subsidiary Bodies (SB64) of the UNFCCC in Bonn from June 8-18. The Bangladesh delegation was led by the special assistant to the prime minister of the newly formed government. As in previous years, I had the opportunity to follow the climate discussions and negotiations at SB64 and engage in a dialogue with the special assistant on Bangladesh’s future climate strategies.
Our exchange highlighted an important opportunity: Moving beyond the narrative of vulnerability and positioning Bangladesh as a global leader in climate solutions.
Bangladesh’s experience, particularly in community-led adaptation and resilience-building, offers valuable lessons for the world. At the same time, the country has an opportunity to further strengthen its role in global climate action by combining adaptation leadership with innovation, collaboration, and strategic engagement.
Based on discussions and reflections from SB64, five priorities deserve particular attention as Bangladesh prepares for COP31.
Bangladesh's greatest climate success story is not found in international conference halls but in local communities.
Over the last decades, investments in cyclone preparedness, community-based disaster management, early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, and local adaptation initiatives have dramatically reduced climate-related mortality and strengthened resilience across vulnerable regions.
These achievements are increasingly recognized internationally as examples of successful adaptation in practice.
However, Bangladesh has not always been effective in translating these experiences into global influence. Stronger documentation, monitoring, and communication of adaptation outcomes are needed.
Robust data demonstrating how local adaptation initiatives reduce vulnerability, improve livelihoods, and strengthen resilience can help position Bangladesh as a global knowledge leader.
At a time when many countries are struggling to operationalize adaptation goals, Bangladesh possesses evidence and experience that the world urgently needs.
Adaptation will rightly remain Bangladesh's highest climate priority. Yet adaptation and mitigation should not be viewed as competing agendas.
The most successful climate investments increasingly deliver both emissions reductions and resilience benefits. Renewable energy systems can strengthen energy security during climate-related disruptions. Nature-based solutions such as mangrove restoration can simultaneously store carbon, reduce disaster risks, and protect livelihoods. Climate-smart agriculture can improve food security while reducing emissions.
By prioritizing mitigation projects that generate adaptation co-benefits, Bangladesh can strengthen its international position, attract additional financing, and demonstrate how developing countries can pursue integrated climate action.
Rather than choosing between adaptation and mitigation, Bangladesh can show how the two agendas reinforce one another.
Climate action is most effective when it is co-created. Bangladesh has a vibrant ecosystem of NGOs, community organizations, researchers, youth groups, social enterprises, and local governments working on climate issues. Yet these actors are not always fully integrated into national climate planning and implementation processes.
Future climate strategies should place greater emphasis on collaborative governance, participatory planning, and co-development. Citizens and local communities possess valuable knowledge about risks, vulnerabilities, and practical solutions. Their involvement improves both legitimacy and effectiveness.
International experience increasingly shows that climate transitions succeed when governments act not only as regulators but also as facilitators of collaboration between public, private, academic, and civil society actors.
As climate negotiations become increasingly complex, effective participation requires a diverse range of expertise.
Bangladesh has long been respected within the UNFCCC process, particularly on adaptation and climate justice. However, future negotiations will increasingly involve highly technical discussions around climate finance, carbon markets, technology transfer, loss and damage mechanisms, and implementation frameworks.
To maximize influence at COP31 and beyond, Bangladesh should continue expanding the diversity of expertise within its delegations. Alongside government officials, delegations can benefit from economists, scientists, legal experts, finance specialists, communication professionals, and experienced negotiators.
Strong climate diplomacy requires both technical knowledge and strategic negotiation skills.
Prepare for emerging carbon market opportunities
The operationalization of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement is creating new opportunities for international carbon trading and climate finance.
Many developing countries are now positioning themselves to benefit from emerging carbon markets through high-quality mitigation projects, nature-based solutions, and capacity-building initiatives. Bangladesh should actively prepare for this evolving landscape.
This requires investments in institutional capacity, transparent governance systems, project development expertise, monitoring frameworks, and stakeholder engagement. Universities, research institutions, private sector actors, and local communities all have important roles to play.
If approached strategically, carbon markets could become an additional source of climate finance while supporting sustainable development objectives.
A new chapter
Bangladesh has already demonstrated that climate vulnerability does not prevent climate leadership. The country's achievements in adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and resilience-building are recognized around the world.
The challenge now is to build on that foundation.
By showcasing community-led adaptation successes, integrating mitigation and resilience objectives, strengthening collaborative governance, enhancing negotiation capacity, and preparing for emerging climate finance opportunities, Bangladesh can help shape the global climate agenda rather than simply respond to it.
As the world prepares for COP31, Bangladesh has an opportunity to present itself not only as a country at risk from climate change, but as a country helping to define the solutions.
Dr Avit Bhowmik is a Climate Scientist and Associate Professor of Risk and Environmental Studies, Karlstad University, Sweden.

item.title: Barman, Koch families allegedly left out of govt ethnic minority survey despite gazette recognition
Men neither see nor listen to women
item.description:
Searching the Dhaka Tribune last week for a piece of my own, I came instead upon an essay I have not been able to put down: Shuchi binte Shahjalal’s The women are divine .
She opens with the old belief of the idol-makers: That a Durga is incomplete unless a little earth from a sex worker’s doorstep is worked into her clay -- for a man leaves his virtue at that threshold, and the ground there turns holy. The goddess cannot be finished without the woman’s soil; the woman herself cannot be let into the festival. The earth is holy, she writes. The person is not.
Let me say at once what I am and am not doing. I am a man, and this is a piece about men. I will not presume to explain to the women of my homeland a cage they have mapped, from the inside, far better than I can.
Shuchi has already said the essential thing, with a scholar’s range and a poet’s aim. I want only to add a footnote -- from the poet we Bengalis reach for whenever we wish to sound reverent about women, and whom, I have come to think, we never actually heard.
We are fond of Tagore as a worshipper of the feminine. We quote him at weddings and drape our daughters’ recitals in his songs. It is worth remembering, then, that at his most attentive, the Bishwakobi was not building the pedestal Shuchi describes. He was warning against it.
I have spent this autumn translating his love songs, one line at a time, and two of them will not now leave me.
The first is Bhalobeshe, sokhi, nibhrite jatone -- “Love me, and in the quiet shrine of your heart, write my name.” Midway, the lover makes a stranger, smaller request:
“Keep, with tender care, my chattering bird, in the courtyard of your palace.”
Read it slowly, and the bird is no ornament. The whole ache of the song is the plea that it be kept, tended, listened to.
In a second song, Tumi ki keboli chhobi -- “Are you only a picture?” -- he almost begs her not to harden into mere paint on a canvas, to be real and present, not an image he can hang on a wall and admire.
A century before our present arguments, Tagore had already named the two ways a man fails a woman: He stops listening to her voice, and he lets her freeze into an image.
Shuchi calls on Nazrul, who dared to address the barangana , the prostitute, as “mother,” and asked who had the right to spit at her.
Let me call on the other giant, who stands, I think, exactly where she does -- on the side of the woman no one will look at or listen to.
Her essay is unsparing about what reverence costs, in life and in death. She recalls the roughly 1,500 women driven from the Kandapara brothel in Tangail in 2014, long after a High Court had ruled such evictions unconstitutional; the sex workers ridiculed when they report rape, because the society “cannot imagine a sex worker being raped”; and Hamida Begum, who in 2020 became the first sex worker in Daulatdia to receive a proper Islamic burial -- after which the imam who prayed over her said he would not do it again, having been scolded by his neighbours.
Beside these, she sets the national figures she cites: By the counts of the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad and Ain o Salish Kendra, 786 women and girls raped in 2025, up from 516 the year before; and almost 22,000 cases of violence against women and children logged by police in a single year.
I will not borrow her numbers to decorate an argument of my own. I note only what she notices -- that behind each is a woman whom a society that sorts its women into goddesses and fallen women has filed under the second heading.
And I would underline, for every man who thinks himself devout, the sentence of hers that ought to be read aloud from pulpits: A society that calls its women mothers and then cannot bury them, cannot hear them, and makes the raped one hide her face while the rapist walks, has not forgotten reverence -- it has made reverence a way to keep women in their place.
Here, let me add the one thing a lifetime in medicine has taught me, because it bears on her point that rape is treated as a stain on a woman’s honour rather than a crime against her body.
I have spent my working life with the human heart -- the actual muscle, four chambers, no holier in a saint than in a so-called fallen woman. A body keeps no ledger of honour. It bleeds the same, grieves the same, heals or fails to heal the same, whatever box the neighbours have assigned its owner.
When we treat a woman’s injury as a stain on her family’s ijjat rather than harm to her person, we are not being moral. We are staring at the honour and refusing to see the woman -- the same failure, once more.
So the answer, I think, is not less reverence but reverence that finally opens its eyes. Read generously, the idol-maker’s belief is almost holy: The goddess is made, in part, of the outcast woman’s earth; the divine and the discarded are the same clay.
The tragedy is only that we stop at the clay. We bow to the figure and walk past the person who gave it her soil.
Tagore points where Shuchi points. Keep the chattering bird -- do not cage it, do not silence it, bend down and listen. Do not let her become only a picture on the wall.
The cure for a goddess no one can bear to meet is not to break her into a “fallen” woman; it is to come down off our own certainty and stand beside her at the doorstep -- to see her face, and to hear her voice.
Shuchi binte Shahjalal has written the diagnosis. The least her countrymen -- and I mean the men -- can do is read it with our eyes open for once, and admit what it took a woman on the Op-Ed desk to say plainly.
The idols are immersed. But the women are still at their doorsteps, many still hiding their faces: Divine in theory, and in practice neither seen nor heard.
Rajani K Saha writes from Stockholm, where he practises medicine.

Rizvi: Nov 7 gave Bangladesh new direction
item.description:
BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi on Saturday said November 7, 1975 revolution and solidarity movement gave Bangladesh a new direction and renewed hope for independence, sovereignty and multiparty democracy.
Nov 7 movement carried three commitments, protecting independence, safeguarding sovereignty and ensuring the continuation of multiparty democracy, and that people took to the streets in July, 2024 with those ideals to defeat what he described as anti-democratic force, he told reporters after paying tributes marking the 51st anniversary of the National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman paid tribute to Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman and former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia at their graves at 8:30am on behalf of the BNP, marking the day.
He said the spirit of November 7 had repeatedly inspired the people of Bangladesh to stand up for freedom, democracy and national sovereignty.
Referring to the political developments of 1975, Rizvi said the country was plunged into anarchy following the events of January 25, when the one-party BAKSAL system was introduced, curtailing people's civil rights.
He said the nation was subsequently pushed into a period of uncertainty and bloodshed, while Ziaur Rahman and his family were detained at their cantonment residence ahead of November 7.
According to Rizvi, people were then deeply concerned about the restoration of BAKSAL, the loss of civil liberties and restrictions on the press.
Rizvi said now some quarters are attempting to disrupt the country's democratic journey by creating instability.
"Sometimes you see crude bombs and cocktails being exploded inside alleys. Instructions are reportedly coming from a neighbouring country while people acting as hired killers and receiving money are trying in various ways to disrupt Bangladesh's democratic journey," he said.
Rizvi said the people would appropriately resist such attempts.
He also warned that the public is observing the activities of different political parties and those trying to take advantage of the situation by creating confusion.
He said people would not forgive anyone who attempted to mislead them or obstruct the democratic process.
Rizvi said the BNP and its supporters remained committed to resisting all undemocratic and anti-national forces, drawing inspiration from the spirit of the Revolution and Solidarity Day.
He said the party would work alongside the people to protect their civil liberties and maintain the continuity of the country's development and production.

item.title: Dhaka’s air quality 4th worst in the world Saturday morning
item.description:
Dhaka, the overcrowded capital city of Bangladesh, has ranked 4th on the list of cities with the worst air quality with an AQI index of 189 at 9:08am on Saturday.
Dhaka’s air was classified as "unhealthy", according to the air quality and pollution city ranking.
India’s Delhi, Pakistan’s Lahore and India's Kolkata occupied the first, second and third spots in the list, with AQI scores of 539, 273 and 198, respectively.
When the AQI value for particle pollution is between 101 and 150, air quality is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", between 150 and 200 is "unhealthy", between 201 and 300 is said to be "very unhealthy", while a reading of 301+ is considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks to residents.
The AQI, an index for reporting daily air quality, informs people how clean or polluted the air of a certain city is and what associated health effects might be a concern for them.
The AQI in Bangladesh is based on five pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), NO2, CO, SO2, and ozone.
Dhaka has long been grappling with air pollution issues. Its air quality usually turns unhealthy in winter and improves during the monsoon.

item.title: 'I thought he'd come back': Jesus on Ronaldo retirement
item.description:
Portugal coach Jorge Jesus said on Friday he had expected Cristiano Ronaldo to return to the national team despite their highly publicised rift, but respected the veteran forward's decision to retire from international football.
Ronaldo, 41, announced on Thursday that he would not play for Portugal again, bringing the curtain down on a record-breaking international career after a bitter end.
"Of course I thought he would come back, of course I thought I would call him up, of course I thought I would speak with him, but you have to respect him," Jesus told reporters after naming his squad for upcoming Nations League matches against Denmark and Wales.
"He decided that it was the moment to leave the national team."
Ronaldo made his debut for Portugal in 2003 and went on to play a world record 234 times for his country, scoring 146 goals.
But his speed and edge have been blunted with age and he fell out with Jesus at the end of September.
The five-time Ballon d'Or winner accused the coach of broken promises after asking him to warm up during a match against Norway without bringing him on. Ronaldo immediately left the team camp and was handed a 30-day suspension and token fine.
He apologised and it was rumoured he intended to return to the Portugal fold, but Ronaldo instead said that he had played his last match for his country.
"Sooner or later it had to happen. He felt it was the best moment to leave, and we have to respect that, while never forgetting what he represented for Portugal," said Jesus.
The 72-year-old coach, who previously managed Ronaldo at Saudi club Al-Nassr, said the interests of the national team had always been his top priority.
"All my decisions were made with the team in mind," said Jesus.
"I do not feel guilty in any way about his departure."
Portugal, who have already secured their place in the Nations League quarter-finals, host Denmark in Braga on November 14 before travelling to Wales three days later.
Jesus handed first call-ups to Monza striker Gustavo Varela, currently Serie A's leading scorer, and Porto right-back Alberto Costa, while Nuno Mendes and Francisco Conceicao miss out through injury.
Uncapped teenagers Rodrigo Mora and Geovany Quenda return to the squad, as does Club Brugge striker Carlos Forbs, who made his debut last year.

Food, medicine shortages choke 3,000 patients at Barisal hospital
item.description:
Around 3,000 inpatients at Barisal Sher-e-Bangla Medical College Hospital face the risk of losing their daily meals as the institution has received no government allocation for food supplies since July.
The hospital, which has 1,000 beds, treats around 5,000 patients daily, including 2,500–3,000 inpatients and more than 2,000 outpatient visitors.
Hospital authorities have so far managed to continue food supplies through the contractor at the director’s request. However, eggs were dropped from patients’ meals on October 15 to reduce costs. The director warned that food supplies could be suspended from March if the government allocation does not arrive.
Hospital Director Brigadier General Dr AKM Mashiul Munir told Bangla Tribune that the contractor had been asked to continue supplying meals despite the lack of funds since July.
“We have reduced the food cost by Tk15 per patient. There was no scope to remove anything else from the menu except eggs. Eggs will be added again once the allocation arrives. If the government funding does not come, we will have no option but to stop food supplies from March,” he said.
The hospital is the main healthcare facility for people across the six districts of Barisal Division, while patients from neighbouring districts also seek treatment there.
Despite its 1,000-bed capacity, around 3,000 patients are admitted daily. More than 1,000 patients receive treatment on floors, while additional beds have been arranged in corridors, balconies and open spaces. Even critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) sometimes have to receive treatment on the floor.
The director said 978 additional beds had been arranged in open spaces to improve patient management.
With two to three attendants accompanying each patient, around 10,000 people are present at the hospital daily, disrupting movement and the treatment environment.
Patients are also facing shortages of essential medicines and diagnostic supplies. X-ray films and medicines required for thyroid tests are unavailable, while CT scans have remained suspended due to a lack of necessary supplies despite the machine being operational.
Medicines for cancer and other complex diseases have also been in short supply for a long time, while some major surgeries cannot be performed.
Hospital sources said the monthly government allocation is insufficient to cover even 11 days of expenses for the current patient load.
Eight of the hospital’s 13 lifts are also out of order. Five of the nine lifts in the old building and three of the four in the new building are non-functional, making it difficult to move patients between floors.
Relatives often have to wait for long periods to take critically ill patients on trolleys to different floors.
Munir blamed the Public Works Department (PWD) for delays in repairing the lifts, saying repeated requests had failed to resolve the problem.
However, PWD Sub-divisional Engineer Md Rasheduzzaman said estimates for the repairs had already been sent to the relevant authorities. Work would begin after funding approval and the appointment of a contractor through a tender process.
The director also expressed concern over declining hospital revenue, blaming irregularities among staff and the outsourcing of diagnostic tests that could be conducted in-house.
He said the hospital should conduct tests on around 1,100 patients daily but currently manages only 500, despite having a target of 2,000.
As a result, hospital revenue has fallen by half compared with the previous year, he added.
Munir said he had taken several initiatives to restore discipline, including arranging additional beds and reorganising wards, but a lack of cooperation had hindered progress.

Three bodies found in Teknaf hills amid ongoing joint operation
item.description:
Law enforcement agencies have received information about three bodies lying in the remote hills of Hnila union in Teknaf, Cox’s Bazar, and are making efforts to recover them.
Joint forces operations in the area are continuing following the killing of an army soldier during a gunfight with an armed human trafficking syndicate.
Police received information about the bodies in the hills between Nayapara and Leda Rohingya camps on Friday afternoon.
Cox’s Bazar Superintendent of Police ANM Sajedur Rahman confirmed the matter, saying they had received reports of three bodies in the hills.
“Efforts are underway to recover the bodies, while operations by law enforcement agencies are continuing in the area,” he said.
On Thursday afternoon, a gunfight broke out during a joint forces raid on an armed human trafficking syndicate’s hideout in the hills. Army soldier Titas Sheikh, 27, was killed after being shot by members of the syndicate.
During the operation, the joint forces rescued 56 people and detained six suspected members of the trafficking syndicate. The rescued individuals were handed over to Teknaf Model Police Station on Friday morning.
Expressing deep sorrow over the soldier’s death, the police superintendent said: “We are deeply saddened and shocked by the death of an army soldier who was shot by armed human traffickers while performing his duties.”
He stressed that eliminating such criminal activities required collective efforts from law enforcement agencies and local residents.

item.title: ‘Joy Bangla’, names of 4 national leaders dropped from Coast Guard ships
item.description:
The Bangladesh Coast Guard has renamed 5 of its ships, dropping the name Joy Bangla and those of 4 national leaders, following approval from the Ministry of Home Affairs.
Under the approved changes, BCGS Joy Bangla has been renamed BCGS Adommo Bangla. The 4 vessels previously named after national leaders have also been given new names.
The 4 other vessels have been renamed as follows: BCGS Syed Nazrul to BCGS Firoz Kabir, BCGS Tajuddin to BCGS Nurul Islam, BCGS Mansur Ali to BCGS M Humayun Kabir, and BCGS Kamruzzaman to BCGS Ashraf Siddiqui.
A letter conveying the approval was sent to the director general of the Bangladesh Coast Guard by the ministry’s Border-3 Branch last Thursday.
According to the letter, the ministry approved the renaming following a proposal submitted by the Bangladesh Coast Guard.
The letter stated that the changes had received approval from the appropriate authority. It was signed by Masfika Hossain, senior assistant secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
However, the letter did not specify the reasons for the renaming or the basis for selecting the new names.

item.title: 56 rescued from human traffickers’ hideout in Teknaf handed over to police
item.description:
The joint forces have handed over 56 people rescued from an armed human trafficking syndicate’s hideout in the remote hills of Rongikhali in Teknaf’s Hnila union of Cox’s Bazar to police.
They were handed over to Teknaf Model Police Station on Friday morning.
Meanwhile, the killing of an army soldier by armed human traffickers during a joint forces operation has triggered anger and concern among local residents.
Locals and public representatives have demanded a sweeping operation to dismantle the traffickers’ hideouts across the hills.
Student representatives have also called for human chains at different locations in Teknaf after Friday prayers to protest the incident.
According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), a gunfight broke out on Thursday afternoon during a joint forces operation against human traffickers in the remote hills of Rongikhali.
Army soldier Titas Sheikh, 27, was killed after being shot by armed traffickers during the operation. Five members of the trafficking gang were arrested, and a pistol, a locally made firearm and four rounds of ammunition were recovered.
Personnel from the Army’s 10 Infantry Division, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and police took part in the operation.
Teknaf Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge Saiful Islam said the 56 rescued people had been handed over to police, who were verifying their identities and other details.
Legal proceedings were also underway over the killing of the army soldier, he added.
The OC said police had been informed about plans to organise human chains demanding action against the criminals.
Asaduzzaman, a resident of Faridpur who was among those rescued, broke down in tears while recounting his ordeal.
He said traffickers had held him captive in a makeshift hut in the hills for eight days. Despite attempting to escape twice, he failed. A group of 40 to 50 armed men guarded the hideout, he added.
Asaduzzaman said he had become acquainted with Imamul, a Rohingya imam from the Kutupalong camp in Ukhiya, while working on a bridge in Cox’s Bazar. They later developed a relationship.
Imamul eventually lured him with the promise of a job at the camp and called him there eight days ago. His mobile phone and other belongings were confiscated before he was taken to the hills in a CNG-run auto-rickshaw at night and handed over to the traffickers.
At the hideout, he found more than 50 other people being held captive. That was when he realised he had fallen into a human trafficking gang’s trap, he said.
He added that a trawler was being prepared for a sea voyage two days earlier, with more than 100 people expected to be transported by boat. The traffickers tried to take him and five others to the trawler, but they were left behind due to a lack of space.
"We were scheduled to be trafficked yesterday. Fortunately, the army arrived and rescued us. But it is heartbreaking that a patriotic army soldier lost his life while rescuing us," he said.
Saiful and Mizanur Rahman Sagar, residents of Sebatkhal in Ukhiya who were among those rescued, said a broker named Nurali had handed them over to the traffickers on the promise of jobs.
They later learned from the traffickers that the two of them had been bought for Tk1 lakh, they alleged.
"For five days, we saw four to five new people being brought to the hideout every day. Anyone who tried to speak up was brutally beaten. We were also beaten when we attempted to escape. Later, they tied us up with iron chains," they said.
They added that they were given food only twice a day, consisting of raw pumpkin and lentils, leaving them severely hungry.
"We were supposed to be put on a trawler and trafficked by sea on Thursday. The joint forces rescued us just in time. There was heavy gunfire during the operation. It felt as though a war was going on in the hills," they said.
Nur Alam, a resident of Hnila, said a sweeping operation was essential to dismantle the powerful network of human traffickers.
"Gunshots can be heard in the hills almost every day. Armed traffickers have made the entire area unsafe. Their hideouts have spread across the hills of Baharchhara, Hnila and Whykong. There is no alternative to a coordinated operation to dismantle these hideouts," he said.
Mohammad Ali, acting chairman of Hnila Union Parishad, said the activities of armed groups operating in the hills were increasing day by day, with human traffickers becoming particularly active during the winter season.
"An army soldier was killed in a gunfight at a traffickers' hideout yesterday. What could be more alarming than this? Ordinary people here are virtually helpless in the face of these criminals.
A sweeping operation in the hills is urgently needed to bring the situation under control," he said. Teknaf Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) SM Anik Chowdhury said law enforcement agencies were working to arrest the armed human traffickers operating in the hills.
"No one will be allowed to escape justice after committing a crime. We are also monitoring the planned human chains," he said.
Expressing deep sorrow over the death of the army soldier, the UNO said eliminating such criminal activities required collective cooperation from local residents alongside efforts by law enforcement agencies.

item.title: Salahuddin: People won’t allow AL to engage in politics again
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed on Friday ruled out the possibility of Awami League's return to politics, saying the people would never again allow the party, which he described as oppressive, autocratic, fascist and murderous, to engage in politics in the country.
"Those who shed people's blood to establish fascism, oppressed the people and committed genocide will have no place in the country's politics again," he said while addressing the concluding session of the 104th two-day annual religious conference at Al-Jamiatul Islamiah Azizul Uloom Babunagar in Fatikchhari, Chittagong.
Questioning whether the people wanted the return of those he described as fascist forces, the minister said some were trying to create conditions for their comeback.
"Those who were forced to flee the country in the face of the mass uprising will not be allowed to return and engage in politics here," he said, adding that those responsible for mass killings and repression had yet to express regret or remorse.
Salahuddin said people were united in opposing the political activities of those responsible for mass killings, despite their differences in political views and ideologies.
He also alleged that fascist forces were behind attempts to create unrest in the garment sector.
Addressing those who were creating trouble in the name of movements, the minister urged them to engage in constructive criticism. "You may choose not to cooperate with the government, but do not withhold your cooperation from the people of this country," he said.
He said it had taken 16 to 17 years to free the country from what he described as an autocratic and Islam-hostile regime.
Salahuddin said many Islamic scholars and students had sacrificed their lives during the struggle.
Citing United Nations estimates, he said around 1,400 people had been killed during the July-August mass uprising, adding that nearly 3,000 people had been victims of enforced disappearance during the preceding 16 to 17 years.
"I was also one of them. By the grace of Almighty Allah and through people's prayers, I am still alive," the minister said.
He claimed that around 7,000 people had been killed or subjected to various forms of torture and persecution during that period, while millions had faced harassment through attacks and cases.
Salahuddin said they wanted the country to prosper economically and improve the living standards of Islamic scholars (ulema) and students of Qawmi madrasahs.
He also alleged that some groups use the name of Islam for political gain, although their election manifestos contain no mention of Islamic values. “Although they say one thing, their documents and official records tell a different story,” he said.
"We believe in Islamic values. We are the party that included 'Bismillah' in the Constitution. We follow the nationalist and Islamic values introduced by Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman," the minister said.
"We have built a united Bangladesh where people from all walks of life share a common national identity. We never want to see division among the people of this country," he added.

item.title: BRAC, UNESCO sign agreement to develop creative economy roadmap
item.description:
Efforts to strengthen Bangladesh's creative economy have gained momentum with a new partnership focusing on film, cultural tourism and heritage, as BRAC and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to advance the country's creative sectors.
Asif Saleh, executive director of BRAC, and Susan Vize, head of office and UNESCO representative to Bangladesh, signed the agreement at BRAC Centre in Dhaka on Thursday.
Asif Saleh said: “Bangladesh's culture and heritage – our crafts, music, film and living traditions – are an economic asset we have only begun to tap. This agreement with UNESCO is about changing that: bringing together the evidence and ideas to support the government to build its national strategy and roadmap for a creative economy that creates real jobs, including for the many people already working in it informally.
“At BRAC, we see this as one interconnected ecosystem. Through Aarong's decades of work with artisans, our long-running popular theatre program and our community-based tourism initiative Otithi, we look forward to working with UNESCO, the private sector and others to help the sector grow.”
Susan Vize said: “Bangladesh has a wealth of cultural heritage and creativity that can be harnessed to improve the lives of everyday Bangladeshis from craftspeople to dancers to chefs. We believe this partnership can help identify key pathways to build on this foundation.”
The partnership will support the development of a national roadmap for the creative economy, identifying priorities and practical steps for growth in the short, medium and long term. It will also assess Bangladesh’s existing creative ecosystem to identify opportunities, address gaps and strengthen collaboration among key stakeholders.
The initiative will focus particularly on the film and audio-visual industries, cultural and community-based tourism, film festivals and heritage.
The collaboration will also explore the establishment of a national Creative Cities Network to help cities build on their cultural heritage and creative strengths.
As part of this effort, BRAC and UNESCO will examine the possibility of Dhaka joining UNESCO’s Creative Cities Network, which brings together cities that use creativity and cultural industries to support sustainable urban development.
Through the partnership, BRAC and UNESCO aim to strengthen Bangladesh’s creative industries, expand economic opportunities and livelihoods, and safeguard and promote the country’s cultural heritage.
Also present at the event were KAM Morshed, senior director of advocacy, communications and engagement at BRAC; Moutushi Kabir, chief people and culture officer of BRAC; and Kizzy Tahnin, head of culture at the UNESCO Dhaka Office.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,276 as four die in 24 hours
item.description:
Four more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Friday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,276.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all four of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,171, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 105, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the four new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in Dhaka, with four deaths reported in both the Dhaka division and Dhaka district.
A total of 1,239 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Friday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 236,714.
During the same period, 75 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 24,294.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 210,982 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 202,394 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: APBn member brutally beaten in Rupganj over anti-drug stance
item.description:
An Armed Police Battalion (APBn) member was allegedly lured to an isolated area and brutally assaulted by suspected drug traders in Rupganj, Narayanganj, for speaking out against drug activities.
The attackers allegedly beat Abul Kalam with sticks and locally made weapons, breaking his arms and legs and severing a tendon in one of his legs. He is now undergoing treatment at the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopaedic Rehabilitation (NITOR) in Dhaka.
The attack took place around 11pm on Thursday in the North Masabo area of Tarabo Municipality.
Kalam had reportedly been opposing drug-related activities in the area for a long time and faced threats for helping law enforcers bring suspected drug traders to justice.
A few days ago, he helped police arrest two alleged drug traders, identified as Shahadat and Emdadul. Following the arrests, Shahadat’s younger brother, Shahjalal, allegedly threatened Kalam several times over the phone and in person.
According to the allegations, Shahjalal called Kalam around 11pm on Thursday, saying he needed to discuss something urgent. He then took him towards an isolated wetland near his home, where 10–15 people were waiting.
The group attacked Kalam as soon as he arrived, beating him repeatedly and allegedly breaking his limbs with sticks and locally made weapons. They also allegedly cut a tendon in his leg.
Hearing his cries, local residents rushed towards the scene, prompting the attackers to flee. They rescued Kalam and took him to a nearby private hospital. He was later referred to NITOR as his condition was serious.
Rupganj Police Station Officer-in-Charge AHM Salahuddin said he had heard about the incident but had not received a written complaint. Police would take legal action after investigating if a complaint was filed.

item.title: 7 Bangladeshi scientists elected TWAS fellows
item.description:
Seven Bangladeshi scientists have been elected fellows of the World Academy of Sciences (TWAS), while Professor Kamrun Nahar has received the prestigious TWAS-Fayzah M Al-Kharafi Award for her contributions to scientific research.
The announcements were made at the academy's recent annual general meeting, held online.
A total of 87 scientists from around the world were elected TWAS fellows this year. The seven Bangladeshi researchers, all members of the Bangladesh Academy of Sciences (BAS), were selected for the 2027 term.
The newly elected fellows are:
Professor Nahar also received the TWAS-Fayzah M Al-Kharafi Award in recognition of her contributions to environmental and agricultural science research. Her selection as a fellow and receipt of the award mark a double recognition by the international academy.
The academy's international jury and executive council recognised the Bangladeshi researchers' contributions to geology, groundwater protection, agricultural science, pharmaceutical chemistry, environmentally friendly jute technology, computer science and quantum physics.

item.title: Applied Human Science College students demand principal's resignation
item.description:
Students of Government College of Applied Human Science, formerly known as Home Economics College, staged a sit-in for a second consecutive day on Friday, blocking the road in front of the institution in Dhaka's Azimpur and demanding the principal's resignation and an investigation into alleged police assaults on students.
They issued a 72-hour ultimatum for the fulfilment of their two-point demands, warning that they would continue their movement until the demands were met.
The protest began at 8am on Friday, with students chanting slogans including “Home Economics has risen”, “Why were police on campus? We want answers” and “Why was my sister injured? We want answers”.
Their first demand is the resignation of Principal Professor Meherunnessa. They said classes and examinations would remain suspended and the principal would not be allowed on campus until she submits a written resignation.
Their second demand is an investigation into the police operation at the college and its residential halls late on Wednesday night, including allegations of baton charges and assaults on students. They also demanded an update on the investigation within 72 hours and punishment for those responsible.
The protest began on Thursday morning, when students gathered outside the principal's office at around 10:30am and later locked her inside by putting a padlock on the office door.
Police arrived at around 11:30pm and rescued the principal after nearly 13 hours. However, more than 100 students continued their demonstration outside the college until around 2:30am.
Students alleged that police dragged female students down the stairs by their hair, beat them and charged at them with batons during the operation.
Several students were injured, according to the protesters, with three to four receiving hospital treatment. One student, who was allegedly trampled by police, is being treated at Dhaka Medical College Hospital.
The protesters also alleged that police entered the residential halls and assaulted students. They further claimed that officers took away several students' mobile phones and identity cards.
The students said the movement was not politically motivated but stemmed from their opposition to the principal's alleged arbitrary decisions and misconduct towards students. They said several of their classmates had been injured, with some still receiving treatment at hospitals.
Although the students had resume their sit-in at 8am on Friday, they said they would allow scheduled recruitment examinations to take place. However, they demanded that the principal be barred from entering the campus during the examinations.
The dispute began over a farewell program held at the college auditorium before the Puja holidays.
According to students and college administration sources, postgraduate final-year students from five departments across three residential halls were initially allowed to hold the program until 10pm. Following their request, the deadline was extended to midnight, but the event continued until 5am.
Principal Meherunnessa subsequently decided to cancel the residential hall seats of two students who coordinated the program, citing the use of the auditorium beyond the permitted time.
Students alleged that when the two approached her to apologise, she demanded Tk12,600 to cover the auditorium's air-conditioning and electricity costs for the night as a condition for reinstating their residential seats.
The principal, however, denied the allegations.
Speaking to journalists on Thursday evening, Meherunnessa said the students had been permitted to hold the programme until midnight but continued until 5am.
She said she initially cancelled the residential seats of the two students over the violation but later softened her position after they apologised. However, she decided to recover the cost of electricity wastage to maintain discipline.
“What the students are saying is the total opposite of what happened. I allowed them to hold a programme until midnight. They continued until 5am. I became a little angry and cancelled the residential seats of the two students,” she said.
Responding to the demand for her resignation, she said: “They are asking me to sign my resignation on a blank sheet of paper. Why should I resign to them?”
Lalbagh police station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Jamil Hossain said students were staging a sit-in demanding the principal's resignation.
“The situation is calm. Police are present at the scene,” he said.

item.title: Kumarkhali loses Tk 35C in potential farm output annually to waterlogging
item.description:
Around 1,250 hectares of cultivable land in Kumarkhali upazila of Kushtia remain waterlogged for seven to eight months every year, causing an estimated annual loss of Tk35 crore in potential agricultural production.
The upazila, surrounded by the Padma, Gorai, Kaliganga and Dakua rivers, has around 18,240 hectares of cultivable land. Farmers can grow crops on the waterlogged land only once a year during the Boro season, producing around 6,225 tonnes of paddy.
If the waterlogging problem is resolved, the land could produce an additional 10,000 tonnes of paddy and other crops during the Aman and Aus seasons, with an estimated market value of Tk35 crore.
Agricultural officials and local farmers say food production could increase further if modern farming methods and high-yielding crop varieties were introduced.
Farmers said although the upazila had numerous irrigation canals under the Ganges-Kobadak (G-K) Irrigation Project, managed by the Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), there was no proper drainage system.
Many canals have remained neglected for years, while some have been filled in to build houses and others blocked by dams for fish farming.
As a result, land that could produce crops three times a year remains submerged for seven to eight months, severely affecting agriculture.
Farmers said the problem continued for nearly a decade without any effective initiative to resolve it. This has reduced agricultural production and caused recurring financial losses for farmers.
A visit to the wetlands of Bahalbaria, Chandpur, Banshara, Bakhai, Karatkandi and Jagonnathpur found large areas under water. Stagnant water was covered with water hyacinths, water spinach (kolmi) and water lilies. Some locals were seen fishing from small boats, while others cleared weeds to prepare their land for cultivation this season.
Many farmers have turned to fish farming by digging ponds after suffering repeated losses from crop cultivation. Ponds have also been dug along canals near the wetlands, while houses and roads have been built in the areas.
Poor maintenance has also left many canals unable to drain water properly.
Rabiul Islam, a farmer from Bahalbaria Beel in Nandolalpur union, said he owned 16 bighas of land.
"Ten to 12 years ago, water used to flow through a canal into the Gorai River, allowing us to grow rice three times a year. Now, as water cannot drain out, we can barely grow even one crop," he said.
Majed Ali, another farmer from the same area, said it was frustrating that water remained stagnant despite the presence of four nearby rivers.
"The stagnant water is covered with water hyacinths and weeds. Clearing them requires six labourers per bigha. Farming has become costly, but yields and profits remain low," he said.
Abdus Samad, a farmer from the Gobindapur Beel area, said some areas had no canals, while existing ones were clogged with weeds and silt.
As a result, water remains trapped on the land, allowing farmers to cultivate crops only once a year.
He said planned excavation of canals could help farmers grow crops three times a year.
Azahar Biswas, a farmer aged over 60, owns three bighas of land in Karatkandi Beel under Sadki union.
He said farmers were struggling because of the lack of proper drainage channels.
A single harvest produces around 12 to 14 maunds of rice per bigha, but the income is almost entirely spent on clearing weeds, Azahar said.
"If we could cultivate the land two or three times a year, farming would become profitable," he added.
According to the local Department of Agricultural Extension office, around 1,250 hectares of the upazila's 18,240 hectares of cultivable land are currently waterlogged.
Of the affected land, 290 hectares are in Nandolalpur union, 250 in Sadki, 240 in Jagannathpur, 205 in Shelaidaha, 75 in Jadu Boyra, 120 in Kaya and 70 hectares in Chapra union.
The waterlogging is affecting agricultural production and making it difficult to meet the upazila's overall food production targets.
In 2024, the area of waterlogged land was only 510 hectares, according to the office.
Upazila Agriculture Officer Md Monir Hossain said the extent of waterlogging had increased over the years with rising rainfall.
He said around 1,250 hectares of land were currently affected, producing only 6,225 tonnes of paddy during the Boro season.
If the land could also be cultivated during the Aman and Aus seasons, farmers could have produced an additional 10,000 tonnes of crops, worth around Tk35 crore, the official said.
He added that the issue had been brought to the attention of the local administration and higher authorities.
Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Md Raisul Islam said proposals for excavating two canals in Kumarkhali had been submitted under the government's ongoing canal excavation project.
Once the excavation work begins, the waterlogging problem will be partly reduced, he said.
Further initiatives would be taken after discussions with local public representatives, the DAE, farmers, the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) and the BWDB, the UNO said.

item.title: Putin slams 'political' moves to keep Russia out of sport events
item.description:
Vladimir Putin on Thursday slammed countries who oppose reinstating Russia into international sports as several European teams said they will refuse to play them at next year's world ice hockey championships over the Ukraine war.
Denmark, Norway, Sweden and the Czech Republic on Tuesday all followed Finland in saying they would not play Russia at the 2027 world championships to be held in Germany.
Russia has been banned from International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) events since Putin launched the 2022 war in Ukraine, but the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled in favour of admitting them to the world championships.
Russia has been mostly banned from international sport since 2022 but some restrictions have eased in recent months -- a trend slammed by Ukraine.
Putin praised the International Olympic Committee and CAS for "taking decisions to uphold the Olympic Charter and its principles", as restrictions have been eased.
"Unfortunately, however, not all countries are prepared to honour the commitments they once undertook, and restrictions on Russian sport -- which are political rather than legal -- continue," Putin told a televised government meeting.
Amid the ice hockey stand-off, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday Russia would not be allowed to compete at next month's World Junior Hockey Championships.
The world championships are due to be held in Germany next May, but the draw and scheduling for the tournament have already taken place, without Russia.
Putin has regularly appeared playing ice hockey during his long presidency.
Russia's war against Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands, forced millions to displace and is Europe's worst conflict since World War II.

item.title: Gold price drops by Tk2,739 per bhori
item.description:
Gold prices in Bangladesh fell by Tk2,739 per bhori on Friday, a day after a major increase, according to the Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus).
The new prices came into effect at 10am on Friday.
Under the revised rates, 22-carat gold is priced at Tk2,26,937 per bhori (11.664 grams), down from Tk2,29,676 on Thursday.
The price of 22-carat gold has been set at Tk19,455 per gram.
The new rates were announced following a meeting of the Bajus Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring on Friday morning.
The association said the prices were adjusted in response to a decline in the price of pure gold in the local market.
According to the revised rates, 21-carat gold is priced at Tk18,580 per gram, 18-carat gold at Tk15,955, and traditional-method gold at Tk13,035.
Bajus has also reduced silver prices.
Under the new rates, 22-carat silver is priced at Tk300 per gram, 21-carat silver at Tk290, 18-carat silver at Tk250, and traditional-method silver at Tk190.
Bajus said making charges will vary depending on the design of the jewellery.
VAT is included in the prescribed selling prices, so jewellers cannot charge it separately from customers.
For exchanges of old gold jewellery, a 12% deduction will apply to the prescribed price after excluding making charges and stone prices.
For purchases of old gold, an 18% deduction will apply.
VAT cannot be deducted separately in either case.
The revised prices will remain in effect at all jewellery shops across the country until further notice, Bajus said.
Gold prices in the domestic market have been adjusted 133 times this year, with 64 increases, 68 reductions and one VAT adjustment.
In 2025, Bajus adjusted gold prices 93 times, raising them 64 times and lowering them 29 times.
The number of price adjustments has increased significantly compared with last year, as fluctuations in pure gold prices in international and local markets have prompted frequent changes in domestic rates.

item.title: Dhaka air quality ‘very unhealthy’ Friday morning
item.description:
Dhaka's air quality turned ‘very unhealthy’ on Friday morning, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 203 at 8:40am.
With this score, the capital ranked fourth among the world's most polluted cities, according to the AQI scale.
A ‘very unhealthy’ air quality level means everyone, regardless of their health condition, may experience more serious health effects or discomfort from air pollution. Even short-term exposure can affect anyone.
Pakistan's Lahore topped the list with an AQI score of 456, followed by India's Delhi with 251 and Kolkata with 221.
On Thursday, Dhaka ranked fifth among the world's most polluted cities, recording an AQI score of 174 at 10:25am.
According to the AQI scale, readings of 101-150 are considered unhealthy for sensitive groups, while scores of 151-200 indicate unhealthy air quality. Readings of 201-300 are classified as very unhealthy, while scores above 301 are considered hazardous and pose serious health risks.
The AQI measures daily air quality and indicates pollution levels and their potential effects on public health.
In Bangladesh, air quality is assessed based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulphur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths worldwide each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.description:
Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) arrested 544 people and filed 62 cases during regular anti-crime operations across the capital in the 24 hours until 8am on Friday.
Of the total arrests, 144 were made in Mirpur Division, 59 in Tejgaon, 44 in Motijheel, 95 in Wari, 41 in Ramna, 49 in Uttara, 42 in Lalbagh and 55 in Gulshan Division.
Another 15 people were arrested by the Special Response Unit (SRU) and the Detective Branch (DB), said Akhtar Hossain, deputy commissioner (Media and Public Relations) of the DMP.
During the operations, law enforcers also seized 540 grams of cannabis, 6,258 Yaba pills, 4.2 grams of heroin in four sachets, 37 Pethidine injections, two knives and two cutters.
Further legal action against those arrested is underway, he added.

PM Tarique’s Khulna visit brings big promises for industry, jobs
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday unveiled plans to develop an industrial corridor stretching from Mongla in the southwest to Panchagarh in the north, seeking to revive struggling industrial regions, attract investment and create employment through expanded port facilities, energy infrastructure and improved connectivity.
During a daylong visit to Bagerhat and Khulna, he laid the foundation stone of a Tk4,068 crore project to expand and modernise Mongla Port, witnessed the signing of an investment cooperation agreement with a Chinese state-owned company and pledged to reopen closed factories while encouraging the establishment of new industries.
The prime minister also assured workers that a new minimum wage would be fixed within one or two months, as garment workers continued demonstrations across several industrial areas demanding higher pay.
Addressing a roadside meeting at Katakhali intersection on the Khulna-Mongla highway, Tarique said his government wanted to restore Khulna’s former industrial prominence and extend industrial development across Bagerhat, Kushtia, Chuadanga and other districts towards Panchagarh.
He said the government would gradually develop the necessary electricity, gas and transport infrastructure to attract factories and generate employment along the proposed corridor.
Earlier, the prime minister laid the foundation stone of the Tk4,068 crore Mongla Port expansion and modernisation project, which includes two container jetties and supporting infrastructure to increase cargo-handling capacity and improve services.
Speaking at the ceremony, he described Mongla as a potential economic hub for the country’s southwestern and northwestern regions.
He said modernising the port would help expand trade and industrial activities in Khulna, Bagerhat, Satkhira and Jashore while strengthening economic connectivity with northern districts.
The government also plans to improve road links between Panchagarh and Mongla, expand port supply chains and facilitate cargo transportation.
According to the prime minister’s deputy press secretary, the project would enable direct container train services between Kamalapur Inland Container Depot in Dhaka and Mongla Port once the necessary facilities are operational.
Tarique also identified the development and operation of Khan Jahan Ali Airport as a government priority.
He stressed that the project’s success would depend not merely on completing infrastructure but also on reducing cargo-handling costs, improving efficiency and attracting investment.
At Mongla Port, the prime minister witnessed the signing of a memorandum of understanding between Invest Bangladesh and China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) on economic and infrastructure cooperation.
Invest Bangladesh Member (Industrial Zones) Saleh Ahmed and China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation Chairman Li Chongyang signed the agreement.
The cooperation framework covers potential investment in energy, industrial and environmentally sustainable infrastructure, transport, logistics and human resource development.
Tarique later held discussions with a Chinese delegation led by CRCC Chairman Dai Hegen.
He urged Chinese investors to establish industries around Mongla and emphasised the importance of reliable electricity and gas supplies for industrial expansion.
The prime minister also thanked the Chinese delegation for supporting opportunities for Bangladeshi workers to secure employment with Chinese companies in the Middle East.
The prime minister said the government wanted to reopen closed mills and factories, including state-owned establishments, and encourage domestic and foreign investment to create employment.
Later, he visited the shrine of Hazrat Khan Jahan Ali in Bagerhat, where he offered prayers.
In Khulna, he inaugurated the second season of Notun Kuri Sports at the district stadium, highlighting the importance of sports, arts and cultural activities alongside academic education.
He said the government was committed to fulfilling its election promises and developing the next generation through education and extracurricular activities.
Around 1.6 million children are participating in the nationwide sporting initiative, according to the program details provided.
The prime minister also reiterated that his government would continue efforts to strengthen the economy despite global challenges.

Health minister: Five Dhaka hospitals to launch PPP-based healthcare services
item.description:
Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Thursday said the government plans to launch improved healthcare services under a public-private partnership (PPP) model, initially at five hospitals in Dhaka on a trial basis.
“Plans are underway to expand the healthcare program to other cities,” he said while addressing an event held at Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Medical College Hospital (SZMCH) in Bogra.
The health minister said discussions with the five hospitals had been finalised, but another meeting would be held next week to determine the fees private partners would charge. The pilot program would begin once financial arrangements were settled, he added.
"We will initially introduce the program on a trial basis at five hospitals in Dhaka before expanding it to other cities. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is interested in the initiative, and we are working to implement it," he said.
Describing SZMCH as a major healthcare centre for northern Bangladesh, the minister said the government was considering expanding access to advanced treatment for complex diseases, including cancer and liver conditions.
Hospital authorities had been asked to submit written lists of their problems, which would be addressed gradually, he added.
On the shortage of doctors and the absence of a separate paediatric ICU at SZMCH, the minister said the government planned to establish around 20 new ICUs across the country, including one in Bogra. He said 17 of the 500 newly appointed doctors had been posted to different healthcare facilities in Bogra, with more appointments planned.
Recruitment of another 5,000 doctors is also underway. Applications have closed, and the Public Service Commission is conducting the interview process, he added.
Blaming corruption and mismanagement over the past 17 years for the deterioration of the healthcare sector, he said the current government was working to restore discipline and improve services.

item.title: QS Asia Rankings: DU retains top position from Bangladesh, 16th in South Asia
item.description:
Dhaka University has retained its position as the top university in Bangladesh in the QS World University Rankings: Asia 2027, securing 136th place among Asian universities and 16th among those in South Asia.
The UK-based international higher education and research organization Quacquarelli Symonds (QS) published the rankings on November 3. DU also held the top position among Bangladeshi universities in last year's rankings.
According to a press release issued by DU, a total of 1,722 universities from 26 countries across Asia have been included in this year's rankings. The University of Hong Kong secured the first position, followed by Peking University of China.
The QS Asia University Rankings assess universities based on several indicators, including academic reputation, faculty-student ratio, research quality and impact, the proportion of staff holding PhD degrees, international research collaboration, and the number of international faculty members and students.
DU Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr ABM Obaidul Islam expressed his satisfaction over the university's position in the international rankings. "This position in the international rankings is a matter of joy and pride for us. Consistently retaining the top position among Bangladeshi universities is recognition of collective efforts of our teachers, students, researchers and all concerned," he said.
However, he said the university's goal was not merely to maintain its ranking but to further strengthen its position internationally through improvement in the quality of education and research.
The vice-chancellor said enriching the academic and research environment, expanding research facilities, strengthening international collaborations and creating opportunities for students to develop globally competitive skills were among the university's key priorities.
